title: Cup and saucer (gobelet litron et soucoupe)

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of John L. Cadwalader, 1914
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A small porcelain cup with a handle, resting on a matching round saucer. Both pieces are decorated with flowers.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, maker, date, medium, tags (Flowers), dimensions, credit line, public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record

context: A cup and saucer made in 1776 at the Sèvres porcelain manufactory, the French royal factory near Paris. The Met lists soft-paste porcelain as its material. The cup is about 7 cm tall and the saucer about 13.7 cm across.

descriptions.k: This is a tiny cup with a saucer under it. They are made of shiny porcelain and decorated with flowers. The cup has a handle. Can you find the flowers? What would you drink from a cup this small?
descriptions.g12: This cup and saucer were made in France in 1776. They are made of soft, creamy porcelain. Flowers decorate them. The cup is only about seven centimeters tall, so it fits in your hand. Look for the handle and the round saucer. Why might someone keep something this small and pretty?
descriptions.g35: This cup and saucer come from Sèvres, a porcelain factory near Paris that made fine tableware for the French king and wealthy buyers. It was made in 1776 from soft-paste porcelain, and flowers are part of its decoration. The cup is only about seven centimeters tall. Compare the cup and saucer. How are their shapes alike, and how do they work together?
descriptions.g68: Sèvres was the French royal porcelain factory, and in 1776 its tableware was a symbol of wealth and fashion. This set is soft-paste porcelain, a glassy material made differently from the hard-paste porcelain of Meissen. The cup, called a gobelet litron, and its saucer carry floral decoration. How do the small size, the handle, and the matching saucer show that this was designed for use as well as show? What might its owner have wanted others to notice?
descriptions.g910: This 1776 cup and saucer from Sèvres shows how a royal factory turned everyday drinking vessels into luxury goods. The restrained cylindrical form of the cup and the matching round saucer provide a stable frame for floral decoration, which was a favorite subject in the period. Soft-paste porcelain, a glassy body distinct from hard-paste, gave Sèvres its recognizable soft look. Consider how scale, matched parts, and surface decoration signal status as well as function.
descriptions.g1112: Sèvres cups and saucers such as this one of 1776 sit at the intersection of technology, patronage, and fashion. Soft-paste porcelain, favored in France before hard-paste became dominant there, allowed distinctive surfaces; the flowers named in the Met record connect it to a widespread taste for floral ornament. The piece is small and domestic, yet its manufacture depended on royal support and specialized labor. Ask how such objects construct ideas of refinement, and what the museum setting hides about everyday use.

g1112.meaning: How do floral motifs on tableware negotiate between decoration, nature, and the display of wealth?

teacherNote.context: Sèvres was the French royal porcelain manufactory and a leader in European luxury tableware. The Met dates this cup and saucer to 1776 and describes the material as soft-paste porcelain.
directions: Have students design a cup and saucer with a matching flower motif and explain how the two pieces connect.
Ask students to compare this set with a cup in their home and discuss which features show status and which show function.
Discuss why a royal factory would make such small, delicate objects.
